newsitem.title: UK: LME copper hit by tightness, others tag along.
newsitem.headline: LME copper hit by tightness, others tag along.

text.p: A bout of tightness hit LME copper on Tuesday morning, injecting some energy into a directionless market as players scrambled to cover positions.

Spreads flared in nearby dates, three months hopped above the psychological $2,300 per tonne barrier and most of the other metals hitched a ride higher. The exception was aluminium, where another sizeable inventory decline gave that market some individual impetus.
Traders welcomed the renewed activity after several days of thin volume and aimless trading.

In ring trading, the premium of cash copper over the May contract was bid as high as $35 a tonne in panicky trading by those with exposed positions. The cash/May spread was slightly in contango last week until Friday when it flipped into backwardation.
The benchmark cash/threes spread traded up to an $85 backwardation, from $60/$65 at the close of business on Monday and in the $30's last week.
Floor traders offered a range of views on what sparked the sudden tightness in nearby dates.
Some said a large player was squeezing the market, with one trader mentioning a large U.S. investment bank, while others said the main impetus was panic covering by influential shorts.
"I think we could see cash/May up to $40 or $50 (backwardation) by the time it's all over," one said.
A few traders shrugged it off as genuine tightness prompted by a congestion of positions. "We've seen this before in the run-up to Third Wednesday pricing," one said.
The constriction centred on April 29 until May 6, with little borrowing seen in the second half of May, traders said.

The three month market skipped up to a high of $2,308 on the pre-market, but struggled in ring trading to hold its stance above the big figure, dipping to end the morning kerb at $2,299, up $10.50 on the day.
Chartists say the market is likely to encounter stiff and staggered resistance from here and must breech the April 9 high of $2,313 and then $2,320 to improve the technical situation.
Aluminium marched higher after stocks fell by 4,700 tonnes, touching a peak of $1,586. It ended the morning with a $24 gain at $1,579.
Tuesday's stocks fall trimmed the total to 818,300 tonnes, down 15.5 percent from its January peak around 968,000 tonnnes.
Much of the recent draws have come from UK warehouses and traders say the material appears to be moving to the U.S. and the Far East.
On the charts, Tuesday's gains have sent the market through the 10-day moving average and within striking distance of the 100-day average at $1,597.
Most of the other metals appearing to be taking a free ride with copper and could just as easily slip back if copper loses momentum, traders said.
Nickel has already shown the fragility of any move higher by jumping to $7,450 in early activity, but falling back to end the kerb unchanged at $7,380.
Dealers noted Eramet's comments that there could be problems if unions continued to block its ferro-nickel and nickel matte exports from its New Caledonia facilities.
Zinc gained $8 to $1,255 but was trapped in a miniscule $3 range, while tin added $60 to $5,770.
Lead touched $638 then settled for a $8 rise at $636.
Alloy finished at $1,462, up from $1,447/50 on Monday.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom ++44 171 542 8065
